claims.text: PbTe can be used as the semiconductor matrix for investigating lattice heat conductivity.
Introducing nanoscale short-range-order precipitates into PbTe will reduce phonon scattering time.
Reduced phonon scattering time will decrease the measured lattice thermal conductivity of PbTe.
The initial PbTe is homogeneous and lacks significant precipitate features.
Lattice heat conduction in the initial PbTe is dominated by long-mean-free-path phonons.
Controlled doping followed by thermal treatment can create nanoscale SRO precipitates in a PbTe matrix.
The intervention will form nanoscale SRO precipitates distributed throughout the PbTe lattice.
SRO precipitates act as scattering centers for heat-carrying phonons.
Scattering by SRO precipitates reduces phonon lifetime and mean free path.
Enhanced phonon scattering lowers the lattice component of thermal conductivity.
PbTe containing SRO precipitates will exhibit a statistically significant decrease in lattice thermal conductivity relative to homogeneous PbTe.
The magnitude and significance of the effect depend on precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Excessive precipitate content or very large precipitates may introduce other scattering or percolation phenomena that complicate the thermal response.
Other phonon-scattering mechanisms may contribute to the measured thermal-conductivity response.
Pristine PbTe measured under matching temperature and measurement conditions serves as the control.
TEM and XRD can be used to characterize the presence, size, and distribution of the proposed SRO features.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in lattice thermal conductivity or phonon mean free path relative to pristine PbTe would falsify the hypothesis.
